docs.h: 1. requirements 2. put the jar in place 3. read the start-up report 4. guard your first item 5. now what? trying it before you buy
docs.b: from a jar in plugins/ to a guarded item in under a minute. estimated time: 3 minutes · paper 1.21+ · java 21 1. requirements paper 1.21 or newer (or a fork with the same api). java 21 . no other plugin. the sqlite, mysql and postgresql drivers ship inside the jar. optional integrations luckperms is used when it happens to be installed and is never needed. the one optional bridge is smartspawner; without it itemguard works exactly the same. 2. put the jar in place plugins/ itemguard.jar # drop it here (or in plugins/itemguard/) start the server. on the first run the plugin creates plugins/itemguard/ with: config.yml — the configuration, fully commented. translations/ — one editable message file per language, nine in all. itemguard.db — the sqlite record. nothing leaves the machine. 3. read the start-up report every start prints one block that says it all — the first thing to look at when something is not working: itemguard v1.0.0 — by sriruma & srpinkyy state: active | 7 tracked item(s) server: paper 1.21.1 (build 133) java: 21.0.12.1 database: sqlite (plugins/itemguard/itemguard.db) language: en loaded: 7 items, 2 template(s) integrations: none | smartspawner sealed ground: on, swept every 30s, 3 reclaim attempt(s) access: per-node (17 nodes) when it cannot start, it names the problem and a fix, instead of stopping on one generic line: itemguard v1.0.0 — by sriruma & srpinkyy state: failed | the plugin was disabled server: paper 1.21.1 (build 133) engine: mysql problem: cannot open the database on mysql 8: access denied for user 'root' try: check the database block of config.yml the engine is named on purpose a wrong password, a missing schema and an unreachable host have nothing in common as a fix. the database line names the engine really in use, with any password= redacted. 4. guard your first item hold a diamond sword and run — with the operator, or itemguard.add granted: /ig create sword this stores the item as template sword . hand a guarded copy to a player: /ig give steve sword amount 64 that copy now has a unique id and cannot be dropped or picked up by anyone but steve. where is it? /ig find ti-1a2b3c drop it on the ground and seal it into place — bedrock below, a label above: /ig seal ti-1a2b3c /ig reclaim # its owner takes it back out nobody can run commands yet? every permission defaults to false , so on a real server operators hold nothing until granted. see permissions . on a test server where everybody joins as operator, set console.ops-are-admins: true and operator status becomes the whole policy. 5. now what? the full /ig command reference every option in config.yml seals, bedrock and the reclaim budget the seventeen nodes and itemguard.admin trying it before you buy builtbybit runs a trial server with the plugin already installed, so you can try it in game before you decide. you join it from the plugin's own listing.

docs.h: reference the shape of the commands a real session the console alternatives and variations
docs.b: everything is done through /ig (alias /itemguard ). a player sees the result on a screen; the console gets text. run /ig help in game for the same list, and /ig help gui for it as a menu. 22 subcommands · info , list and flag open a screen for a player reference command what it does /ig create <template> [force] create or overwrite a template from the item in hand /ig delete <template> delete a stored template /ig unlink [id|hand] stop tracking an item; the item itself is untouched /ig give <player> <template> [amount <n>] [flags k=v] [raw] [quiet] build and deliver an item /ig transfer <player> [id|hand] send a tracked item to another player /ig owner <player> [id|hand] [raw] transfer an item and its ownership /ig flag <template|id|hand> [flag=value ...] read the flags on a screen, or change them /ig recover <id> take an item back wherever it is, in one piece /ig regenerate <id> [confirm] rebuild a lost item from its stored copy /ig reclaim [id] the owner takes their own sealed item back /ig seal <id|hand> seal an item lying on the ground /ig unseal <id> take a seal off without moving the item /ig find <id> report where an item is /ig tp <id> [confirm] teleport to the item: the placed block, the copy on the ground, an online holder, or a container it can see. if none of that is visible it names the reason and waits for confirm /ig info <id|hand> [history] the record on a screen; history opens the event list /ig list <templates|items> the catalogue or the tracked objects, on a screen /ig version itemguard, server and java versions /ig permissions every itemguard node you hold, with a yes or a no /ig integrations the database engine and the optional integrations /ig reload reload config, messages, templates and data /ig help [gui] the full list, as text, or as a read-only menu the shape of the commands options may be written in any order. id means a tracked id such as ti-1a2b3c ; hand means the item currently in hand. the shorthand is permissive: wherever an id is needed, hand works. piece meaning example id / hand refer to an item by id or by the item in hand /ig flag hand droppable=true flags k=v ... pin one or more flags on one delivery only /ig give steve sword flags droppable=true recoverable=false raw deliver without the count, or transfer ownership without moving the item /ig owner alex ti-1a2b3c raw quiet suppress the recipient's notification /ig give steve sword amount 64 quiet confirm accept a potentially-lossy step (tp or regenerate) /ig tp ti-1a2b3c confirm a real session /ig create sword /ig give steve sword amount 64 /ig find ti-1a2b3c # in steve's inventory /ig seal ti-1a2b3c # steve drops it, you seal it /ig reclaim # steve takes it back /ig info ti-1a2b3c # the whole story, on one screen the console the console is blocked by default : it may only run the subcommands listed in console.allow , which defaults to give . that is what lets a store plugin such as tebex fulfil a purchase without being handed full control. console: allow: - give a few read-only subcommands bypass the list entirely: version , reload , help , integrations , permissions and allow . none of them can create, move or delete a tracked item, which is what makes them safe. /ig allow is the console view of the allowlist. not sure who can run what? /ig permissions prints every node with a yes or a no and needs no permission of its own — the people who need it are exactly the ones who cannot run anything else. see permissions . alternatives and variations /ig help gui — the command list as an in-game chest menu, reading only. same facts, different surface. hand everywhere — you rarely need to type an id: /ig info hand , /ig seal hand , /ig unlink hand . screens — /ig info , /ig list and a bare /ig flag open a menu for a player instead of printing. see in-game screens .

docs.h: the seven flags where a flag lives reading and writing flags flags on a single delivery worked variations
docs.b: a flag is a behaviour switch with a conservative default. seven of them decide what a protected item is allowed to do — nothing more, nothing less. precedence: the item wins, then the template, then the default the seven flags flag default meaning droppable false the holder may drop the item on the ground pickupable false anyone, including the owner, may pick it up movable true it may be moved between inventories by click or drag hopper-transfer true a hopper may pull the item out of a container breakable-by-others false someone other than the owner may break the placed block explosion-protected true a container explosion rescues it rather than destroying it recoverable true a lost copy may be rebuilt by /ig regenerate “off” is the conservative direction for a loss; “on” for a movement drop, pickup and breaking by others are the losses itemguard exists to prevent, so their flags default to off. moving between your own slots and an explosion's blast were never stopped by the plugin and cost nothing, so movable , hopper-transfer , explosion-protected and recoverable default to on — each keeps exactly the freedom itemguard had before flags existed. where a flag lives a flag can be set at three levels, and the more specific one wins: item — pinned on a single tracked item. template — inherited by every item created from it. default — the conservative value above. an item that stops pinning a flag falls back to the template, and a template that stops pinning one falls back to the default. nothing gets stuck. reading and writing flags /ig flag sword # the seven flags, on a screen /ig flag sword droppable=true # pin the flag on the template /ig flag ti-0123 pickupable=true recoverable=false /ig flag ti-0123 droppable=template # fall back to the template again without a value, the command is a report, and for a player it is a screen: every flag with its value, the layer that value came from, the default, and one sentence on what it does — the fastest way to answer “why does this item behave like this”. the console prints the same facts as text. see in-game screens . it is read-only on purpose. a menu of toggles would let one stray click decide how an item behaves, and an item that cannot be picked up is the sort of bug nobody could trace back, so changing a flag stays a sentence with a value in it. flags on a single delivery /ig give accepts the same flags k=v option to pin values on one delivery only, without touching the template: /ig give steve sword amount 64 flags droppable=true recoverable=false quiet handy for event items you want to fall to the ground but never be stolen, or giveaway items that become returnable on death. worked variations scenario flags a spawner nobody may ever take droppable=false pickupable=false movable=false hopper-transfer=false breakable-by-others=false explosion-protected=true recoverable=true a cosmetic item for events, allowed to be dropped droppable=true pickupable=false breakable-by-others=false a key that must be passable between staff droppable=false pickupable=true movable=true hopper-transfer=false a quest item that may be genuinely lost recoverable=false pickupable=false and the ground an un-pickupable item that gets dropped lies in the open forever: nobody can pick it up, not even the owner. that is what seals are for — the dropped item gets a bedrock seat and a label, and the owner takes it back with /ig reclaim .

docs.h: the idea creating and managing delivering from a template examples a staff-only vault key a spawner that survives everything variations worth knowing
docs.b: a template names a group of items and carries the flags they share. every item created from it is guarded the moment it lands — no per-item configuration to maintain. create from the item in hand · overwrite with force the idea a template is a stored copy of the item you held when you ran /ig create , plus a set of flags. when you /ig give from it, the delivered copy is an instance of the group: it inherits the template's flags; it carries its own unique id, so it is tracked independently; it can override any single flag without touching the group. when the staff upgrade a spawner, the new one is guarded the moment it lands. when they add a second vault key slot, they add one template and every future key behaves. creating and managing /ig create sword # template "sword" from the item in hand /ig create sword force # overwrite it (keeps the name, takes the shape) /ig delete sword # remove it /ig list templates # everything stored without force , creating a name that exists is refused rather than silently replaced. delivering from a template /ig give steve sword amount 64 reads as “make a sword for steve”: the item is built from the template, a fresh id is written into its nbt, and the owner is recorded. options: option effect amount <n> deliver a count instead of the template's default flags k=v ... pin flags on this delivery only raw deliver without a count (a single item, however it is shaped) quiet do not notify the recipient a template is a policy, not a pile changing a flag on the template changes future deliveries; it does not rewrite items already in the wild. items pin their own overrides, so a one-off variant costs nothing. see flags for the precedence. examples a staff-only vault key /ig create vaultkey # with a named item in hand /ig flag vaultkey pickupable=true movable=true hopper-transfer=false /ig give alex vaultkey keys pass between staff (pickupable, movable) but can never be hoppered away or lost to a drop. a spawner that survives everything /ig create spawner /ig flag spawner explosion-protected=true recoverable=true breakable-by-others=false /ig give steve spawner amount 1 flags movable=false the group is theft-proof by default; this delivery is also immovable, and only this one. variations worth knowing rename-proof — the template name is a key, not a label: overwriting with force changes the shape, never the name. deleting a template does not delete items already delivered from it — their records and flags are their own. reloadable — /ig reload picks up template changes without a restart.

docs.h: what ownership means handing an item to a player transferring ownership: the confirmation raw — change ownership without moving the item history
docs.b: the owner is not a name in a record. the owner is who the protections answer to — and that is why moving an item and moving its ownership are two different things that you do together. read on: /ig give · /ig transfer · /ig owner what ownership means the recorded owner is the only player who: may break the block the item was placed as; is rescued for when an explosion hits the container holding it; is queued for when a recovered item arrives on death; may reclaim a sealed item on the ground. transferring an item without transferring ownership would split those: the new holder could walk around with the item while explosions still sent it back to the old owner. handing an item to a player /ig give steve sword amount 64 # build and deliver, steve becomes the owner /ig transfer steve ti-1a2b3c # send an existing tracked item on /ig transfer steve hand # ...or let it come from your hand transferring ownership: the confirmation /ig owner <player> [id|hand] moves both the item and its ownership — but it is confirmed by the current owner, not just by the admin running the command: /ig owner alex ti-1a2b3c -> alex is asked to accept /ig owner confirm -> run by the current owner two rules follow from that: both players must be online. that is the point: nobody can quietly hand an item away from an account that has been hijacked, and nothing gets queued for a recipient who is not there. a request does not survive a restart. an owner coming back days later will not find a stale transfer waiting. raw — change ownership without moving the item /ig owner alex ti-1a2b3c raw for a sale where a middleman passes the item on without ever holding it: the record changes hands, the item stays where it is. history the history belongs to the object, not to whoever held it. a transfer is recorded as transfer with both names, and the old entries are left alone. /ig info <id> opens the item's record on screen, and its history button shows the full event list.

docs.h: what a seal is taking it out for the owner: /ig reclaim for an admin: /ig recover and /ig unseal the seal block in config.yml permissions around seals
docs.b: an item with pickupable=false that lands on the ground would lie there forever: nobody can pick it up, not even its owner. a seal turns that limbo into a place. bedrock under the item · label above it · the item itself is never touched what a seal is when a guarded item ends up on the ground, the plugin lays a block underneath it and places a floating label above it: bedrock where the ground can take one — air, grass, a plant or a snow layer. on bare stone the label appears on its own. a label naming the item, its owner and the command that takes it out. the seal never contains the item: the item itself is untouched, /ig find still locates it, and a lost seal costs nothing but the marker. hoppers, fire, explosions, despawn and liquids are all refused around a seal, and a periodic pass repairs any marker that is damaged or missing. taking it out for the owner: /ig reclaim /ig reclaim # looks for the nearest seal, no id needed /ig reclaim ti-1a2b3c # or name the item the owner gets three attempts per window (24 hours by default), and needs no id — it finds the nearest seal, so an item that was paid for does not have to be looked up first. the budget is not refunded by a success. a successful reclaim does not hand an attempt back: otherwise a player could drop and reclaim the same item forever and the limit would never bind. only the window closing clears it. once the attempts are spent, the seal stays put and an admin takes the item out with /ig recover . for an admin: /ig recover and /ig unseal /ig recover ti-1a2b3c # take the item out, in one piece, wherever it is /ig unseal ti-1a2b3c # take the seal off without moving the item the seal block in config.yml seal: enabled: true # master switch for everything below bedrock: true # lay bedrock under the item where the ground allows it hologram: true # place the label above it sweep-seconds: 10 # how often to look for items to seal and seals to repair reclaim: max-attempts: 3 # attempts the owner gets per window window-seconds: 86400 # how long that window lasts radius: 8.0 # how far /ig reclaim looks when given no id every number is clamped into a range that cannot wedge the server: a negative budget or a zero-length window would either lock every owner out forever or hand out unlimited attempts. sweep and unloaded chunks only loaded chunks are checked by the sweep pass, so an item in an unloaded chunk is sealed the moment someone loads it. set sweep-seconds: 0 to turn the pass off — items already sealed stay sealed but will not be repaired. a bedrock left behind by a seal taken down while its chunk was away is queued and removed when the chunk comes back, so the next seal on that spot can always get a bedrock of its own. permissions around seals itemguard.reclaim is the one permission granted to everyone by default: owning an item is enough to get it back. revoke it on a group and its players are sent to an admin instead. itemguard.seal controls both /ig seal and /ig unseal . see permissions .

docs.h: the nodes two shorthands with luckperms when everybody who joins is an operator finding out what you actually hold
docs.b: every permission defaults to false , so not even operators hold them until they are granted — with one deliberate exception. 18 nodes · itemguard.admin bundles them all the nodes permission allows default itemguard.add /ig create false itemguard.remove /ig delete and /ig unlink false itemguard.give /ig give false itemguard.send /ig transfer false itemguard.owner /ig owner false itemguard.flag /ig flag false itemguard.recover /ig recover false itemguard.regenerate /ig regenerate false itemguard.reclaim /ig reclaim true itemguard.seal /ig seal and /ig unseal false itemguard.find /ig find false itemguard.tp /ig tp false itemguard.info /ig info false itemguard.list /ig list false itemguard.break break a tracked block owned by someone else false itemguard.version /ig version false itemguard.reload /ig reload false itemguard.admin all of the above false the one exception itemguard.reclaim defaults to true so that owning an item is enough to get it back. revoke it on a group and its players are sent to an admin instead. two shorthands itemguard.admin arrives two ways, and itemguard resolves both itself, so they work even without a permission plugin: itemguard.admin — every node at once, also declared in plugin.yml as a children: list for luckperms, vault and friends. itemguard.* — the wildcard prefix, for whatever wildcard support the permission plugin has. with luckperms /lp group default permission set itemguard.admin true granting the seventeen nodes one by one is never necessary. luckperms is not a dependency and is not shaded: itemguard only ever calls sender.haspermission(...) , which every permission plugin implements. when everybody who joins is an operator on a test server, a preview, or anything behind a launcher that gives every player operator, the policy above is a problem: everybody is an operator and no operator holds any of the seventeen nodes, so the owner can install the plugin and still not run a single command. console: ops-are-admins: true operator status becomes the whole policy. it defaults to false and it does not touch the permissions: a non-operator is refused exactly as before. two choices worth knowing: read once, at start-up. /ig reload does not change it, so /ig permissions can never contradict itself. a refusal tells an operator about it. denied operators are shown the switch; everyone else just sees the missing node, because for them the node is the answer. finding out what you actually hold /ig permissions prints every node with a yes or a no, plus the name of the message file in use. it needs no permission of its own, because the people who need it are exactly the ones who cannot run anything else. when a subcommand is refused, the message names both the node and the subcommand: you do not have itemguard.add, which /ig create needs.

docs.h: the blocks at a glance lang server-id database protect-placed-blocks seal console logging placeholders in item names and lore reload
docs.b: the commented config.yml shipped with the jar is the documentation of record. this page goes block by block, with the defaults and the variations. written to plugins/itemguard/config.yml on first start · /ig reload re-reads everything the blocks at a glance lang: default # message language server-id: '' # written on first start; do not edit database: # sqlite | mysql | postgresql protect-placed-blocks: true seal: # seals, bedrock, sweep, reclaim budget console: # allowlist and ops-are-admins logging: # console / file / detail lang lang: default default is english. choose es , de , fr , pt-br , it , pl , nl or ru . any value the plugin does not ship falls back to english with a warning in the console. see translations . server-id server-id: '' the plugin writes a random id here on first start and the database remembers the one that claimed it. it is what enforces one-database-per-server, so do not edit it by hand. see database . database database: type: sqlite # sqlite | mysql | postgresql host: localhost port: 0 # 0 uses the engine's default: 3306 or 5432 name: itemguard user: "" password: "" params: "" # e.g. "sslmode=require" or "usessl=true&requiressl=true" the last five values are only read for mysql and postgresql. a plain-text password sits here, so keep the file out of version control. see database . protect-placed-blocks protect-placed-blocks: true stops other players from breaking blocks that belong to tracked items (chests, spawners, …). these can always break them: the owner of the item; whoever holds itemguard.break . explosions do not destroy these blocks either. false restores the old behaviour, where anyone can break them and recover the item. seal seal: enabled: true bedrock: true hologram: true sweep-seconds: 10 reclaim: max-attempts: 3 window-seconds: 86400 radius: 8.0 explained in full on seals & reclaim . every number is clamped so a bad value cannot wedge the server. console console: allow: - give ops-are-admins: false allow is the list of subcommands the console may run — the store-plugin safety valve. ops-are-admins is the test-server switch. both are covered on permissions . logging logging: console: true file: false detail: normal file: true writes every line to plugins/itemguard/logs/yyyy-mm-dd.log as well as the console; detail: verbose also writes the debug lines. file logging is off by default because a file nobody reads just grows. placeholders in item names and lore item names and lore support these placeholders, in both a long and a short form: long short becomes %ti_id% {id} the unique id of the tracked item %ti_template% {template} the template it was created from %ti_owner% {owner} the player the item was delivered to — {player} the current holder — {amount} the default amount for the template — {date} the current date reload /ig reload re-reads config, messages, templates and data, so a change takes effect without a restart. one value is deliberately read once at start-up: console.ops-are-admins , a server-wide policy that must never contradict /ig permissions mid-session.

docs.h: the nine languages why a folder of its own how editing works colour codes one yaml trap
docs.b: every message the plugin shows to a player comes from a file you can edit. nine languages ship on board, and each message documents the placeholders it accepts. plugins/itemguard/translations/ · english is en.yml like the rest the nine languages value language default english ( en.yml ) de german es spanish fr french it italian nl dutch pl polish pt-br brazilian portuguese ru russian set lang: in config.yml to switch. any value the plugin does not ship falls back to english with a warning in the console. why a folder of its own on first start the folder translations/ is created with all nine files, and they are yours to edit: change the wording, the colours, add a line. they live in their own folder so they cannot be lost together with the database — a translation file sitting next to itemguard.db is one rm away from being deleted with it. english is en.yml like the rest, so all nine files sort together and none is special-cased by name. how editing works your copy wins for every key it has. a key that a new version added — and that your file does not have yet — is read from the bundled file, so there is nothing to delete after an update, and no raw keys in chat. /ig reload re-reads them without a restart. upgraded from an older version? files a previous version kept in the data folder root as messages.yml , messages-<code>.yml (or the hand-renamed messages_<code>.yml ) are moved into translations/ under today's names on the first start after the upgrade, so your custom wording survives. a file that already exists in the folder always wins — nothing is overwritten. colour codes text supports & colour codes, hex colours as &#rrggbb , and named placeholders between braces, such as {id} , {player} , {amount} or {what} : give: ok: "&allegó {player}: &f{amount} × {item} ({id})" # comments in the file # document the placeholders a key accepts every key in en.yml documents in a comment which placeholders it accepts, so whoever edits the messages does not need to read the code. one yaml trap yes and no are booleans in yaml 1.1 so a key named after one of them makes the message come out as its own name. rename the key rather than quoting the value — quoting works on the file you see, but the fallback read from the jar follows the same rule and would disagree.

docs.h: the screens the record screen why the flags screen is read-only the layout nothing can be taken out an item that is gone
docs.b: a player is told things on a screen, not in chat. chat is scrolled past; a menu is read. 5 screens · 35 entries a page · nothing clickable out four commands open a screen for a player, and print for everyone else: /ig info <id|hand> # the record /ig info <id> history # the event list /ig list items # every tracked object /ig list templates # the catalogue /ig flag <target> # the flags, read-only the console has no inventory to open, so it gets the text output instead. nothing about the rules changes: a screen shows the same data the command would have printed, and it re-reads that data every time it is drawn. the screens screen opened by what it is for items /ig list items every tracked object, one icon each, most recently seen first record /ig info <id> , or an icon on the items screen state, owner, template, coordinates, dates and id, all on one screen history the history button on the record the last fifty events, newest first flags the flags button, or /ig flag <target> all seven flags: value, where the value came from, what each one does templates /ig list templates the store's catalogue; an icon opens that template's flags the record screen three rows. the object itself in the middle of the top row, with the whole record on its tooltip. the facts people look up separately — owner, template, location, state, flags, history — as their own icons in the second row. and in the third row, what can be done to it. icon does the item nothing. the record, on its tooltip: state, owner, template, created, where and when it was last seen, and the id player head the owner, named book the template it was made from; click it for that template's flags compass where it was last seen: world, x, y, z and the date knowledge book its state comparator its flags written book its event history spyglass, ender pearl, beacon, anvil, iron block find, tp, recover, regenerate, seal — only for a player who holds the matching permission arrow, clock back to the list, and redraw this screen from the database a button runs the command as the player who clicked it, so the permission check, the confirmation prompt and the message are the command's, and there is only one of each. a button a player has no permission for is not drawn at all rather than drawn and refused: a menu full of dead buttons is a menu nobody trusts. action buttons close the screen before running. a confirmation asked behind an open inventory is a question nobody sees, and a screen showing pre-action data is worse than no screen. the seal button follows the item, not just the permission. a sealed object gets “take the seal off” and an unsealed one gets “put a seal on”. a lost object has nowhere to put a seal, so the button is greyed rather than offered. why the flags screen is read-only changing a flag is /ig flag <target> flag=value — a sentence with a value in it. a row of toggles would let one stray click decide how an item behaves, and an item that cannot be picked up would be the sort of bug nobody could trace back. so the screen shows the seven flags with their value, the layer that value came from, the default, and one sentence on what the flag does, and changing one stays a command. the layout the same on every screen, so learning one teaches all of them: row 1 entries, close barrier in the top right corner row 2 row 3 row 4 row 5 black row 6 previous .......... page .......... next every slot a screen is not using is a black stained-glass pane . an empty slot in the middle of a table does not read as “end of the data”, it reads as a broken item — so the panes go in first and the content is written over them. the barrier is in the same corner on every screen, because it is the one position that is the same on a two-row detail screen and a six-row list. lists hold 35 entries a page. where there is no previous page, the arrow is still there and greyed out rather than absent: a control that appears only sometimes is a control players have to look for. nothing can be taken out every

docs.h: sqlite by default mysql and postgresql one server per database, enforced running several servers, or moving one
docs.b: one database per server, by design. your shop server, your faction server and your hub keep three separate copies of the guard — and the plugin enforces it, because it is the only way the data keeps its meaning. sqlite out of the box · mysql and postgresql for a bigger disk, your own backups, or a second machine sqlite by default a single file at plugins/itemguard/itemguard.db , no database server, nothing leaves the machine. the right choice until you can say why not. back it up with the same routine that backs up the world; like the world, it changes while the server runs, so back it up from a file-level snapshot rather than by copying a live file. mysql and postgresql database: type: postgresql # sqlite | mysql | postgresql host: db.example.net port: 5432 # 0 uses the engine's default, 3306 or 5432 name: itemguard user: itemguard password: "" params: "sslmode=require" # tls through a proxy, in the standard form the jdbc drivers are inside the plugin jar — nothing else to install. the tables are created on the first start; the account only needs rights on its own schema. params carries the usual connection strings, e.g. sslmode=require or usessl=true&requiressl=true . the password is never logged: the start-up line prints the url with it masked, and a password= parameter you add by hand is redacted too. a plain-text password sits in config.yml . keep that file out of version control and out of screenshots. one server per database, enforced each install keeps a server-id in its config.yml , generated on first start, and the database remembers the one that claimed it. a second server that points at the same database is refused on its first start , with a message naming the install that owns it. why enforce rather than document it: these tables are full of world names and coordinates, and a world name is not a coordinate until you know whose world it is. with two servers sharing one database, /ig find would report a chest that is not there, /ig tp would walk an admin over to the wrong place without complaining, and the seal sweep would lay bedrock under coordinates that mean something else — all silently. one database per server is the only way those three commands are allowed to say what they mean. running several servers, or moving one running several servers? give each one its own schema on the same mysql or postgresql server (one create database each) and each jar its own config.yml . moving a server to new hardware? copy the whole plugins/itemguard folder — server-id included — and it carries on. editing the id by hand turns the install into a different server in the one way that matters, and its own database will say so on the next start-up. the engine in use is printed on start-up and shown by /ig integrations .

docs.b: the questions that come up most often, answered short. what does it need to run? paper 1.21 or newer and java 21. no other plugin is required: the sqlite, mysql and postgresql drivers ship inside the jar, and luckperms is used when installed but never needed. does it support spigot, forge or fabric? itemguard is a paper plugin. it needs the paper api at 1.21 or newer; a fork with the same plugin api works, and paper itself is the supported target. do i need a database server? no. sqlite is the default: a single itemguard.db file, nothing leaves the machine. mysql and postgresql are supported when you outgrow a file. either way, one server per database — enforced, not advised. see database . can i run the same plugin on two servers with one database? no, and the plugin refuses instead of silently misbehaving. its tables are full of world names and coordinates, which only mean something to the world they came from. give each server its own schema. where is the item’s id kept? in the item’s nbt, written at delivery time. the record in the database says where it is; the two are kept in step, and the plugin never drops items on the ground or duplicates them. why can’t my players pick up or drop their bought item? because droppable and pickupable default to off — a conservative default, so protection is on from the first delivery. a dropped un-pickupable item is sealed where it falls and the owner takes it back with /ig reclaim . give away what you mean: see flags . what happens when a container with my item explodes? if explosion-protected is on (the default), the block survives and the item with it. when an item is genuinely lost, a recoverable copy can be rebuilt with /ig regenerate , or pulled back from wherever it is with /ig recover . someone bought something and it is gone. how do i make it right? ask for the facts: /ig info <id> opens the item's record, and the history button on it opens the full event list, including the last place it was seen. then decide between /ig recover (take it back in one piece) and /ig regenerate (rebuild it from the stored copy). who counts as the owner, and how does a sale get handed over? the owner is the one protection answers to: the only one who may break the placed block, the one explosions rescue the item for, and the one sealed items return to. /ig owner hands the item and its ownership over, confirmed by the current owner — nobody can quietly move an item out from under a hijacked account. see ownership & transfer . how do i let my store plugin fulfil purchases without full admin? the console is blocked except for the subcommands in console.allow , which defaults to give — a store plugin such as tebex can run /ig give <player> <template> and nothing else. read-only commands ( version , reload , help , integrations , permissions , allow ) bypass the list. why does nothing work—i’m an operator and i still get refused? every permission defaults to false , for operators included. grant itemguard.admin , or on a test server where everyone joins as operator set console.ops-are-admins: true . /ig permissions shows exactly what you hold. see permissions . can i change the wording, or translate it myself? yes. every message comes from plugins/itemguard/translations/ , one editable file per language with documented colour and placeholder support, and /ig reload picks changes up without a restart. see translations . is it free, and where do i get it? itemguard is a paid plugin, sold on builtbybit. if you would rather see it run before you spend anything, builtbybit has a trial server with the plugin already installed — you join it from the plugin’s listing. can i try it before i buy? yes. the quick start above is the whole installation; the trial server is for playing with the plugin in game. you join it from the listing on builtbybit. did something break. what do i read first? the start-up block, which prints facts — state, engine in use with credentials masked, and a named problem with a suggested
